title.narrative: HUM Localisation pilot: Start Fund Bangladesh/Start Network
HUM Lokaliseringspilot: Start Fund Bangladesh/Start Network

description.narrative:
Overall objective of the response:
Humanitarian responses are localised, rapid, informed and adapted to the needs of the affected population
SFB will ensure this through the implementation of three areas of programming.
Result 1: Humanitarian action is timely, proactive, contextualised, coordinated, needs-driven, and informed by those closest to crises.
The projects in the fund will address one of three types of humanitarian needs in Bangladesh: underfunded small- to medium crises, forecasts of impending crises, and spikes in chronic humanitarian crises. Projects will start as soon as possible after the funds are disbursed; aiming to reach affected communities with humanitarian assistance within 7 days. It is anticipated that this project will target a total of 27,212 individuals, with 10% of the disaster-affected population being directly assisted through small scale anticipatory response out of the overall population covered by both rapid and anticipatory response. Populations expected to be reached through implementation of member activities are climate-vulnerable, disaster affected communities across Bangladesh.
Result 2: SFB member NGOs have organisational readiness and equal opportunities to access direct funding and influence decisions, thereby fostering a more locally-led, accountable humanitarian response
The SFB secretariat will provide capacity strengthening support to local and national NGO members for organisational readiness as they access funding and actively engage in decision-making. It is expected that approximately six alerts will be raised and implemented under this project; all by local and national NGOs.
Result 3: Humanitarian action is locally informed and generating evidence to influence a more appropriate, effective and efficient humanitarian system
Learnings collected from implementation of SFB pooled fund activations will develop knowledge around best practices that will be widely shared and promoted within the network and through national, regional and global-level coordination mechanisms. Key activities include information sharing, knowledge management and advocacy through national and international platforms.

Start Network is a new cooperation partner for Sida and the planned support from Sida would specifically support Start Network’s national programme called Start Fund Bangladesh (SFB). SFB is a member­-led, rapid emergency response pooled funding mechanism that offers timely financing to people at risk of or affected by small to medium scale crises. The Start Fund's purpose is to reach communities rapidly to alleviate human suffering, enhance resilience, reduce use of negative coping mechanisms, and minimise the loss of assets. The fund is modelled on Start Network’s global Start Fund, which releases funding within 72 hours of a crisis alert and fills a crucial gap in humanitarian funding. It is accessible to local, national, and international member NGOs operating in Bangladesh to respond early to under the radar emergencies. This gives NGOs the ability to respond in a timely and effective way and meet the needs of the affected communities. Support to SFB is considered to contribute to strengthening local and national actors in humanitarian action and to the Grand Bargain's overall efforts to improve and streamline aid.
The overall objective of the contribution: Humanitarian responses are localised, rapid, informed and adapted to the needs of the affected population

title.narrative: Grant Agreement between Sida and Start Network

description.narrative:
The 2024 Annual Review reported on Start Network as a whole but also the programme Start Fund Bangladesh. In 2024, the SFB provided life-saving assistance to over 104,000 people by supporting 11 emergency responses in 23 districts of Bangladesh. As an example, seasonal flooding in Dhaka prompted a crucial response where over 15,000 people in the most affected areas received clean water and hygiene kits to prevent tainted water supplies causing waterborne disease outbreaks in crowded neighbourhoods.
Sida has provided funding to the SFB throughout 2025. During the annual meeting on 14 August 2025, Start Network shared that they had triggered 7 alerts throughout 2025 and implemented 14 projects where 7 of these projects were implemented with Sida's funding. The total funds distributed were £451,001 (£224,003 with Sida's contribution). The projects reached communities within 5.3 days and reached 65,363 people. The projects responded to three floodings, one heatwave, one riverbank erosion, one fire and one dengue outbreak.
Challenges remain in reaching communities in remote areas such as island locations and in the Chittagong Hill Tracts, as well as in areas with political unrest.
As of August 2025, 89% of the total funds distributed for 2025 were directly distributed to local and national non-governmental organisations (LNNGOs). 100% of Sida's contribution has gone to LNNGO member organisations to support communities affected by crisis. LNNGOs participation in project selection and allocation decision-making has increased since last year as 79% of the member organisations that participated in project selection decision making were LNNGOs and 80% of the member organisations that participated in allocation decision making were LNNGOs.
Start Network has made efforts to strengthen the role of local actors in Bangladesh's humanitarian architecture through the following examples. SFB served as Co-Chair of the HCTT Localisation Technical Working Group (LTWG), representing local and national organisations. This led to the representation of local and national NGOs in humanitarian coordination by establishing a dedicated platform for LNNGOs to engage in national-level dialogue and decision-making. Start Network ensured equitable Indirect Cost Recovery (ICR) sharing between INGOs and LNNGOs within Start Bangladesh which enabled a global policy shift on equitable partnership across Start Network members worldwide. Start Network also supported capacity development and organisational planning for 22 local organisations across multiple districts in Khulna and Coxs Bazar. The development and implementation of organisational development plans, led to the improvement of internal policies and regulatory compliance for more accountable and structured operations.
Sida visited SFB's operations during 2025 and concluded that local participation is seen as an asset throughout the whole cycle of the SFB programme. In fact, decision-making from local partners was an actuality and a good showcase of what locally-led humanitarian action should look like. Alert types that SFB responds to are those that are overlooked by larger responses which shows that the SFB covers a gap in the humanitarian response in Bangladesh. The structure of SFB is lean and this is a comparative advantage as well as the speed for decision-making and implementation. Sida has found that the partnership with Start Network and particularly, support to SFB, provides significant learning opportunities for Sida which Sida will continue to explore.
